stem: A latency-sensitive checkout API is backed by an AWS Lambda function written in Node.js. During traffic spikes, some requests take an extra 1-2 seconds because Lambda must initialize a new execution environment. The team wants execution environments kept initialized and ready before requests arrive. Which configuration BEST addresses this?
options: Configure provisioned concurrency on the function (or a published version/alias) so a specified number of execution environments are initialized in advance.
Set reserved concurrency to cap the maximum number of concurrent executions.
Increase the function's timeout setting so slow initializations do not fail.
Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the function.
explanation: Provisioned concurrency keeps a specified number of execution environments initialized and ready to respond, removing cold-start latency for the invocations that use it. Reserved concurrency only sets a ceiling (and floor) on concurrent executions; it does not pre-initialize anything and can even cause throttling if set too low. Raising the timeout changes how long a function may run, not how fast it initializes. X-Ray tracing adds observability but does not affect cold-start behavior.

stem: A Lambda function processes messages from a standard SQS queue using an event source mapping with a batch size of 10. When one message in a batch causes an unhandled exception, the entire batch is currently retried, including the 9 messages that succeeded, causing duplicate side effects. Which change BEST fixes this while keeping a single event source mapping?
options: Set the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to 1 so batches are processed one at a time.

Enable the function's ReportBatchItemFailures response type and have the function return the identifiers of only the failed messages, so the event source mapping deletes the succeeded ones and retries just the failures.
Reduce the batch size to 1 so every message is processed and retried independently.
Increase the SQS visibility timeout to a very large value so failures never trigger a retry.
explanation: ReportBatchItemFailures (partial batch response) lets the function return exactly which message IDs failed; the event source mapping then deletes the successful messages from the queue and retries only the failed ones, avoiding reprocessing successes. Shrinking the batch size to 1 avoids the symptom but sacrifices the throughput benefit of batching and does not scale to larger workloads. A very large visibility timeout only delays retries; it does not stop successful messages from being redelivered once a retry does happen. Reserved concurrency of 1 serializes processing but does not change which messages get retried.

stem: A team has five Lambda functions across different projects that all depend on the same internal logging and validation utility library. Repackaging the library into every function's deployment package is becoming a maintenance burden. Which Lambda feature lets the team share this code across functions without duplicating it in each deployment package?
options: A Lambda destination configured on each function.
A separate Lambda function that the other functions invoke synchronously for every call.
An environment variable containing the library's source code.
A Lambda layer containing the shared library, attached to each function.
explanation: Layers package shared code and dependencies as a separate .zip archive that can be attached to multiple functions, so the library is maintained once and referenced everywhere instead of being duplicated. Destinations route asynchronous invocation results, not shared code. Calling another function for every invocation adds latency, cost, and a hard runtime dependency between functions. Environment variables hold configuration values, not source code libraries.

stem: A team wants to shift 10 percent of production traffic on an AWS Lambda function to a new version to validate it before a full rollout, while the other 90 percent continues to invoke the current version, without changing the client-facing function ARN. Which approach BEST achieves this?
options: Increase the new version's reserved concurrency to 10 percent of the total.
Publish the new code as a new Lambda version and update the production alias to split traffic between the two versions using weighted alias routing.
Deploy the new code directly over $LATEST and ask 10 percent of clients to invoke a different ARN.
Create a second, separate Lambda function and use Route 53 weighted routing between the two function URLs.
explanation: A Lambda alias can point at two versions at once with an assigned weight, routing a chosen percentage of invocations to the new version while every client keeps invoking the same alias ARN. Overwriting $LATEST removes the ability to roll back cleanly and forces clients to change ARNs, which defeats the goal. Standing up a second function and splitting with Route 53 works for HTTP-triggered function URLs but adds unnecessary infrastructure and does not apply to non-HTTP triggers. Reserved concurrency caps how many concurrent executions a version may use; it does not route a percentage of invocations to a specific version.

stem: An AWS Lambda function is invoked asynchronously by S3 event notifications. The team wants to capture both successful and failed invocation records, including the original event payload and the function's response, and route successes to an EventBridge event bus for downstream processing while sending failures to an SQS queue for investigation. Which configuration meets this with the LEAST custom code?
options: Add a try/except block in the function code that manually publishes to EventBridge on success and to SQS on failure.
Enable AWS X-Ray tracing to capture invocation payloads for later replay.
Configure Lambda destinations: an on-success destination pointing at the EventBridge event bus, and an on-failure destination pointing at the SQS queue.
Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) on the function pointed at the SQS queue and rely on it for both successes and failures.
explanation: Lambda destinations for asynchronous invocations natively route both success and failure records, including the original event and the response or error, to targets like EventBridge, SQS, SNS, or another Lambda function, with no custom code. A DLQ only captures failed events after all retries are exhausted, carries only the original event (not the response), and has no on-success path at all. Manual try/except code duplicates a feature Lambda already provides and adds ongoing maintenance burden. X-Ray captures trace data for debugging, not event payloads for routing to other services.

stem: A team is building a new public API that needs only Lambda proxy integration and JWT authorizers, with low latency, and does not need usage plans, API keys, or request/response transformation via mapping templates. Which API Gateway API type MINIMIZES cost and setup complexity for this use case?
options: A WebSocket API with a Lambda integration.
An HTTP API, which supports Lambda proxy integration and JWT authorizers at lower cost and latency than a REST API.
A REST API with a Lambda proxy integration and a usage plan attached.
A REST API with request and response mapping templates configured.
explanation: HTTP APIs are purpose-built for proxy integrations to Lambda or HTTP backends and for JWT authorizers, and they cost less and have lower latency than REST APIs when the advanced REST API features are not needed. A REST API supports usage plans and API keys, but the scenario says those are not needed, so the extra REST API cost and complexity is unwarranted. Mapping templates are a REST API-specific feature the scenario also does not need. A WebSocket API is for persistent bidirectional connections, not a typical request/response public API.

stem: A developer configures Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda proxy integration for a REST API resource. The Lambda function code parses the incoming event assuming it directly contains the client's JSON request body as top-level keys, but the function throws a KeyError in production. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: API Gateway requires a mapping template to inject the body into the event before proxy integration can work.

With Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway passes the entire request (headers, path parameters, query string, and body) inside a structured event object, and the client's JSON body arrives as a string in the event's body key that must be parsed separately.
Lambda proxy integration silently drops the request body for all POST requests.
The Lambda function must return a plain string instead of a structured response, so API Gateway cannot parse the incoming request.
explanation: In Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway forwards the full request as a structured event where the raw client body is a JSON-encoded string under the body key, alongside separate headers, pathParameters, and queryStringParameters keys, so the function must parse event['body'] itself to get the client's fields. Proxy integration does not drop request bodies. The function's response format (statusCode/headers/body) is a separate, outbound concern and does not affect how the inbound event is structured. Mapping templates are a non-proxy (custom) integration feature and are bypassed entirely in proxy integration.

stem: A company exposes a REST API on Amazon API Gateway to external partners. Each partner must be limited to a different request rate and monthly quota, and the API must identify which partner is calling without requiring a full OAuth flow. Which API Gateway feature combination BEST meets this?
options: Create a separate REST API for each partner with a hardcoded Lambda authorizer per API.
Use a single API key shared by all partners and track usage by partner in application logs.
Configure AWS WAF rate-based rules as the only mechanism to distinguish partners.
Issue an API key per partner and associate each key with a usage plan that defines that partner's throttle rate, burst limit, and quota.
explanation: API keys associated with usage plans let API Gateway identify each caller and enforce per-key throttle rates, burst limits, and quotas without a full OAuth flow. Building a separate API per partner does not scale operationally and is unnecessary since usage plans already isolate limits per key on one API. A shared key cannot distinguish callers for enforcement, only for after-the-fact log analysis. WAF rate-based rules throttle broadly by IP pattern and are not designed to enforce distinct per-partner quotas tied to a caller identity.

stem: A REST API on Amazon API Gateway serves a GET endpoint whose response rarely changes but is called at high volume, driving up backend Lambda invocation cost. The team wants API Gateway itself to serve repeated identical requests from cache for a configurable time, without changing the client or the backend. Which feature should they enable?
options: API Gateway response caching on the stage, with a defined TTL for the cached responses.
AWS Lambda provisioned concurrency on the backend function.
Amazon CloudFront in front of the API with no caching behaviors configured.
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the backend data store.
explanation: API Gateway stage-level caching stores responses for a configurable TTL and serves matching subsequent requests directly from the cache, cutting backend calls with no client or backend change. Provisioned concurrency reduces Lambda cold starts, but the function still runs on every request rather than being bypassed. CloudFront without caching behaviors configured passes every request through, providing no caching benefit. DAX caches DynamoDB reads, which is unrelated to caching the API Gateway response itself.

stem: A DynamoDB table stores IoT sensor readings with device_id as the partition key. A small number of high-traffic devices are producing far more writes than the rest, causing ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors on specific partitions even though the table's overall consumed capacity is well under its provisioned capacity. Which TWO changes would BEST reduce this hot-partition throttling? (Select TWO.)
options: Add a high-cardinality suffix to the partition key (write sharding), such as device_id plus a random or calculated suffix, to spread a single device's writes across more partitions.
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so DynamoDB can scale to accommodate a spike without pre-provisioned partition-level limits.
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity units without changing the partition key design.
Add a global secondary index with the same partition key as the base table.
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table.
explanation: Write sharding, adding a calculated or random suffix to a hot device's partition key, spreads its writes across multiple physical partitions instead of concentrating them on one. On-demand capacity mode lets DynamoDB provision and scale partition-level throughput automatically for unpredictable, spiky access patterns. Raising the table's overall provisioned WCUs does not help because DynamoDB divides capacity across partitions, so a single hot partition can still throttle even when the table has spare aggregate capacity. A GSI with the same partition key inherits the same hot-key problem. Streams capture a change log and have no effect on write throttling.

stem: An application's DynamoDB table uses order_id as the partition key and order_date as the sort key. A new access pattern needs to query all orders for a given customer_id, sorted by order_total, across the entire table, including orders created before this new pattern existed. Which index type supports this?
options: A global secondary index (GSI) with customer_id as the partition key and order_total as the sort key, which can be added after table creation and queries across all items.
A local secondary index (LSI), which must share the base table's partition key and can only be created at table creation time.
A DynamoDB Stream filtered on customer_id.
A scan operation with a FilterExpression on customer_id, run on demand.
explanation: A GSI can use a completely different partition key (customer_id) and sort key (order_total) from the base table, can be added at any time after the table exists, and covers all existing and new items, exactly matching this new access pattern. An LSI must share the base table's partition key and can only be defined when the table is created, so it cannot introduce a new partition key like customer_id after the fact. Streams provide a change log, not a queryable index. A full table scan with a filter works but reads every item and does not scale, so it does not meet the need for an efficient, index-based query.

stem: Two application instances may read and update the same DynamoDB item concurrently. The team wants to prevent one instance's update from silently overwriting a change made by the other, without using a distributed lock service. Which approach BEST achieves this?
options: Enable point-in-time recovery (PITR) on the table.
Maintain a numeric version attribute on the item and perform updates with a ConditionExpression that the version equals the value last read, incrementing it on each successful write.
Always use PutItem to overwrite the entire item on every update.
Increase the table's read capacity so reads never see stale data.
explanation: A version attribute with a conditional write (optimistic locking) makes an update succeed only if the item still has the version the client last read, and fails it otherwise so the caller can retry, preventing silent lost updates with no external lock service. Unconditional PutItem overwrites whatever is there regardless of concurrent changes, which is exactly the problem being described. Higher read capacity affects throughput, not consistency between a read and a later write. PITR restores the table to an earlier point in time for disaster recovery; it does not prevent concurrent write conflicts.

stem: A DynamoDB-backed API serves the same small set of frequently read items thousands of times per second, and both read latency and DynamoDB read costs are higher than the team wants. The team needs microsecond-range read latency without significantly changing application read/write APIs. Which service BEST fits?
options: Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached, queried directly instead of DynamoDB for every read and write.
AWS Global Accelerator in front of the DynamoDB endpoint.
Amazon CloudFront caching of the raw DynamoDB API responses.
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), an in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB and is compatible with the existing DynamoDB API calls.
explanation: DAX is a DynamoDB-specific, write-through in-memory cache that supports the same DynamoDB API calls with minimal code changes and cuts read latency to microseconds for cached items. ElastiCache for Memcached could work but requires the application to build and manage a separate cache-aside pattern and API rather than being a near-drop-in DynamoDB cache. Global Accelerator improves routing to endpoints over the public internet; it does not cache item-level reads. CloudFront caches HTTP content and is not designed to front the DynamoDB service API.

stem: A team needs to synchronize DynamoDB item changes (inserts, updates, and deletes) to an Amazon OpenSearch Service index in near real time, and their processing logic needs to see both the old and new item images to decide what changed. Which combination BEST supports this?
options: Enable DynamoDB Streams with the view type set to capture both new and old images, and configure a Lambda trigger on the stream to process each record and update OpenSearch.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the KEYS_ONLY view type and reconstruct the full item by re-reading it from OpenSearch.
Schedule an hourly AWS Glue job that scans the entire DynamoDB table and re-indexes every item.
Enable point-in-time recovery and query the recovery data for changed items.
explanation: DynamoDB Streams configured for NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES delivers both the item's previous and new state for every change, and a Lambda trigger on the stream processes each record near real time to update a downstream index like OpenSearch. KEYS_ONLY only exposes the key attributes, which is not enough to compare old and new values without an extra read. A full-table Glue re-index every hour is neither near real time nor gives explicit old-versus-new diffs per change. PITR is a backup and restore feature, not a mechanism for streaming ongoing changes.

stem: A DynamoDB table stores session tokens that should be automatically removed 24 hours after creation without the application running a cleanup job or consuming write capacity to delete them individually. Which DynamoDB feature BEST fits?
options: DynamoDB Streams configured to delete old items.
On-demand backups scheduled every 24 hours.
Time to Live (TTL), which reads an expiration timestamp attribute on each item and lets DynamoDB automatically delete expired items in the background at no extra write-capacity cost.
A global secondary index sorted by creation timestamp.
explanation: TTL lets you tag an item with an epoch expiration timestamp, and DynamoDB's background process automatically deletes expired items without consuming provisioned write capacity or requiring application code. A GSI can help query by time but does not delete anything by itself. Streams only capture change events; nothing about a stream deletes items on its own. On-demand backups snapshot the table for restore purposes and do not remove individual expired items.

stem: A worker application polls a standard SQS queue and takes an average of 45 seconds to process each message, but the queue's visibility timeout is set to the default of 30 seconds. The team notices some messages being processed twice. What is the MOST likely cause, and what is the BEST fix?
options: Because processing takes longer than the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and a second consumer picks it up before the first finishes; increase the visibility timeout to comfortably exceed the expected processing time (or extend it dynamically with ChangeMessageVisibility).
SQS standard queues always deliver every message at least twice by design, so no visibility timeout change can prevent it.
The queue's message retention period is too short, causing messages to be redelivered.
The consumer is not using long polling, which causes duplicate delivery.
explanation: When processing time exceeds the visibility timeout, the message reappears in the queue while the first consumer is still working on it, so a second consumer can receive and process the same message: the fix is to size the visibility timeout above the expected processing time or extend it mid-flight with ChangeMessageVisibility. Standard queues do provide at-least-once delivery in general, but the specific, controllable cause here is the timeout being shorter than processing time. Message retention period controls how long an unconsumed message stays in the queue before being discarded, not redelivery during active processing. Long polling reduces empty responses and the chance of missing a message; it does not cause or prevent this duplicate-processing scenario.

stem: A team migrates a payment-processing workload to an SQS FIFO queue to guarantee ordering and exactly-once processing within related payments. Which TWO statements about FIFO queue behavior are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: FIFO queues automatically convert to standard queues once throughput exceeds 300 messages per second, even with high-throughput mode disabled.
A FIFO queue guarantees a message is delivered to a consumer exactly once with no possibility of a consumer receiving it more than once.
Ordering across all message groups in the queue is guaranteed globally, regardless of MessageGroupId.
Messages that share the same MessageGroupId are delivered to consumers in the order they were sent, while messages in different message groups may be processed in parallel.
Content-based deduplication (or an explicit MessageDeduplicationId) lets SQS recognize and discard duplicate sends within the 5-minute deduplication interval.
explanation: Within a single MessageGroupId, FIFO preserves send order, while different groups can be processed concurrently, which is how FIFO queues scale. Deduplication, whether content-based or via an explicit MessageDeduplicationId, drops duplicate sends made within the same 5-minute interval, giving exactly-once send semantics. A FIFO queue does not silently convert to standard; without high-throughput mode it is limited to about 300 (3,000 with batching) transactions per second per API action, and exceeding that throttles rather than converts the queue type. FIFO prevents the queue itself from introducing duplicates, but a consumer that fails to delete a message before its visibility timeout expires can still receive it again, so exactly-once consumer delivery is not absolutely guaranteed. Ordering is only guaranteed within a message group, not across the whole queue.

stem: An order-processing event needs to trigger three independent downstream workflows: updating inventory, sending a confirmation email, and recording analytics, each with its own retry and processing needs, and the team wants to add or remove downstream consumers later without changing the producer. Which pattern BEST fits?
options: Write the event directly to three separate DynamoDB tables from the producer.
Publish the event to a single SQS standard queue and have all three workflows poll the same queue.
Publish the event once to an SNS topic and subscribe an SQS queue for each downstream workflow (the fan-out pattern).
Have the producer call each downstream service's API directly in sequence.
explanation: The SNS fan-out pattern publishes one message to a topic that delivers a copy to each subscribed SQS queue, so each downstream workflow gets its own independent, durable queue with its own retry behavior, and consumers can be added or removed without touching the producer. Calling each service directly couples the producer to every consumer and its availability. Writing to three DynamoDB tables bypasses each workflow's own processing and retry logic entirely. A single shared SQS queue delivers each message to only one consumer, not to all three workflows, so it does not fan out.

stem: A company's order service emits events that several teams' applications need to react to differently: the shipping team only cares about events where detail-type is OrderShipped, and the billing team only cares about events where detail.amount is greater than 1000. The team wants each consumer to receive only the events relevant to it, without the producer knowing about the consumers. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Publish all events to one SQS queue and have each team's application read every message and discard the ones it does not need.
Publish events to an SNS topic and rely on every subscriber receiving every message unfiltered.
Have the order service call each team's API directly with a conditional check on which team to notify.

Publish events to an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus and create a separate rule with an event pattern for each team that matches only the fields that team cares about, targeting each team's own queue or function.
explanation: EventBridge rules use event patterns to match on fields like detail-type or nested detail values, so each team's rule filters and routes only the events it cares about to its own target, decoupling the producer entirely from consumer-specific logic. A shared SQS queue delivers every message to only one consumer at a time and provides no content-based filtering. Plain SNS topic subscriptions without a filter policy send every message to every subscriber, forcing consumers to filter themselves. Direct API calls from the producer reintroduce the tight coupling the team wants to avoid.

stem: A workflow orchestrates a long-running order fulfillment process that can take up to 3 days, must be resumable across that period, and needs a full execution history for auditing every state transition. Which AWS Step Functions workflow type BEST fits?
options: A single long-running Lambda function with a sleep loop to wait 3 days.
An SQS delay queue with a 3-day delivery delay configured.
A Standard workflow, which supports executions up to one year, exactly-once workflow execution semantics, and a full, visual execution history.
An Express workflow, which is optimized for high-volume, short-duration (up to 5 minutes) event-processing workloads.
explanation: Standard Step Functions workflows support executions up to a year, keep a durable execution history for auditing, and are built for long-running, auditable processes like a multi-day fulfillment flow. Express workflows are priced and optimized for high-volume, short-duration workloads (up to 5 minutes) with less granular history. A Lambda function cannot sleep for 3 days within a single invocation because Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes. An SQS delay queue's maximum delivery delay is only 15 minutes, far short of 3 days, and it has no concept of an auditable multi-step execution history.

stem: A clickstream analytics pipeline needs multiple independent consumer applications (real-time dashboards, fraud detection, and a data lake loader) to each read the SAME stream of events in order, replay up to 7 days of history if a consumer falls behind or is redeployed, and scale to very high throughput. Which service BEST fits these requirements over SQS?
options: An SQS FIFO queue with a separate message group per consumer application.
SNS with an SQS subscription for each consumer application, using standard SQS queues.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, where each shard preserves order, multiple independent consumers can read the same records using separate iterators, and a configurable retention period (up to 365 days) allows replay.
A standard SQS queue shared by all three consumer applications.
explanation: Kinesis Data Streams retains records for a configurable period (24 hours by default, extendable up to 365 days) and lets any number of independent consumers read the same records at their own pace using separate shard iterators (or enhanced fan-out for dedicated throughput), matching multiple independent, replay-capable readers of the same ordered stream. A single SQS queue delivers each message to only one consumer, so the other two would never see it. An SQS FIFO queue with different message groups still delivers each message to one consumer overall; message groups control ordering and parallelism within one logical consumer set, not independent multi-reader fan-out. SNS-to-SQS fan-out does give each application its own queue, but standard SQS queues do not support long replay windows or preserve strict, stream-wide ordering the way Kinesis shards do, making it the weaker fit when 7-day ordered replay is a hard requirement.
